candidates.statement: We will review the AMPS argument in section [\[firewallsect\]](#firewallsect){reference-type="ref" reference="firewallsect"} below, but a key point in motivating their setup is a claim that an infalling observer is able to extract information from the Hawking radiation of a black hole prior to falling in.[^2] The model black hole of Hayden and Preskill [@HaydenPreskill], also partially reviewed below, suggests that this should be possible provided that the observer is able to perform a sophisticated nonlocal measurement on the Hawking radiation that has come out so far.
More concretely the real issue at stake is for which types of situations we should trust effective field theory (EFT).
If we wish to maintain belief in unitarity, as AdS/CFT strongly suggests we should, then there must be a more broad set of criteria for when EFT is not be valid.

These results are consistent with a point of view expressed by Aaronson [@Aaronson:2005qu] that the laws of physics should not permit computational machines that radically alter the basic structure of complexity theory.
At most, they should force some marginal changes around the edges, as in the case of Shor's factoring algorithm.
[^7]: There could be "cosmological" restrictions on what Charlie is able to do, but it seems that these should be decoupled from restrictions "intrinsic" to the black hole.

From our discussion of $U_{dyn}$ in section [\[slowcomp\]](#slowcomp){reference-type="ref" reference="slowcomp"} it seems that in a completely pristine environment Charlie should even be able to test unitarity in polynomial time; we won't address whether or not Charlie would be able to do this in a "noisy" environment.
- Because $\mathcal{H}_B$ and $\mathcal{H}_R$ are shared with Charlie, we must have $\rho^{\{Alice\}}_{BR}=\rho^{\{Charlie\}}_{BR}$.

candidates.statement: For [\[strongsub\]](#strongsub){reference-type="eqref" reference="strongsub"} to be consistent with the subadditivity inequality $S_A+S_B\geq S_{AB}$ we then must have $$I_{AB}\equiv S_A+S_B-S_{AB}=0.$$ $I_{AB}$ is called the *mutual information* between $A$ and $B$, and it is zero if and only if the density matrix $\rho_{AB}$ is actually a product $\rho_A\otimes \rho_B$.

candidates.statement: A key step in the AMPS argument is that $B$ and $R_B$ are accessible to both Charlie and Alice and that therefore they must agree on the entanglement between them.
They are related only insofar as they must agree on the results of experiments which are visible to both of them.

We will phrase the discussion in terms of Charlie's Hilbert space, since for the moment we are following AMPS and granting that Charlie and Alice must agree on the density matrix of $\mathcal{H}_B\otimes \mathcal{H}_R$.
candidates.section_title: The AMPS Experiment as a Quantum Computation

candidates.statement: Such a set is called an $\epsilon$-net, and it is not too hard to get an estimate of how many elements it must have [@hayden2004randomizing].
[^2]: In this counting we can easily ignore the constraint that orthogonal states must be sent to orthogonal states.

Restating the setup of the previous section, we can think of the black hole as a polynomial-size circuit $U_{dyn}$ which acts on a set of microstates $|i\rangle$ as $$U_{dyn}|i\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|B||H|}}\sum_{bh}|b\rangle_B|h\rangle_H U_R(i)|bh0\rangle_R.$$ The point here is that we must be able to recover any initial state from the final state, so the unitaries $U_R(i)$ must all be distinct elements of the coset $U(2^n)/U(2^n-2^{m+k})$.

Since each state $|i\rangle$ must have its own distinct $U_R(i)$, the vast majority of initial microstates must be decoded by generic $U_R$'s which necessarily take time of order $2^{n+k+m}$ to implement.

The question of how many bits can be lost without losing the ability to error correct with high probability of success has been studied in the literature, and as discussed in the previous subsection for the erasure channel the number of bits which are lost must be less than $\frac{n-k}{2}$.
This will typically be true for more general codes like the one discussed here as well since they should protect information at least as well as stabilizer codes.

Moreover, only a statistically negligible amount of information should leak from the prover to the verifier. [QSZK]{.sans-serif} is the set of computational problems with yes/no answers for which such a prover can always convince the verifier of yes instances but will fail with high probability for no instances.

[QSZK]{.sans-serif} also trivially contains [BQP]{.sans-serif}, the class of problems that can be solved on a quantum computer: for such problems, the verification can be done directly using the computer itself without any need for a clever discussions with a prover. [QSZK]{.sans-serif} should therefore be understood as the set of problems whose yes instances can be reliably identified using a quantum computer with the help of an all-powerful prover, albeit one who is both secretive and dishonest.

(An efficient quantum algorithm corresponds to a small circuit that can itself be laid out efficiently, a further requirement that should arguably be relaxed in discussions of the AMPS paradox.) It is known that determining whether a function is 1-to-1 or 2-to-1 requires exponentially many calls to the function, even for a quantum computer [@aaronson2002quantum].

In particular if we look for solutions of the Klein-Gordon equation of the form $$\phi\equiv r^{-\frac{d-2}{2}}e^{-i\omega t}Y_{\ell}(\Omega_{d-2})\Psi_{\omega \ell}(r),$$ it is not hard to see that $\Psi_{\omega \ell}$ must obey a Schrodinger-type equation $$-\frac{d}{dr_*^2}\Psi_{\omega \ell}+V_{eff}(r)\Psi_{\omega\ell}=\omega^2 \Psi_{\omega \ell}.$$ Here $r_*$ is a "tortoise" type coordinate obeying $$r_*'(r)=f^{-1},$$ and the effective potential is $$\begin{aligned} \nonumber V_{eff}(r)=R^{-2}\bigg(1+\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^2&-\frac{\alpha R^2}{r^{d-1}}\bigg)\bigg[\left(m^2+\frac{d(d-2)}{4R^2}\right)r^2\\ &+\left(\ell(\ell+d-3)+\frac{(d-2)(d-4)}{4}\right)+\frac{(d-2)^2}{4}\cdot \frac{\alpha}{r^{d-3}}\bigg].\label{AdSPot} \end{aligned}$$ The details of this potential do not matter, but we see that it vanishes linearly at the only real positive root of $f(r)$, that is at the horizon, and that it grows quadratically with $r$ at large $r$.

When we continue to Euclidean time we can set the $\tau$ periodicity of the AdS soliton [\[adssol\]](#adssol){reference-type="eqref" reference="adssol"} freely, but for the black brane [\[bb\]](#bb){reference-type="eqref" reference="bb"} we must choose $r_0$ to be consistent with the $\tau$ periodicity for the Euclidean geometry to be smooth.

candidates.statement: Having fixed $S_0$ we can also derive an interesting bound on the AdS radius $R$ in Planck units: we know that we must have $T>L^{-1}$ to avoid starting the computation below the phase transition discussed in the previous section, so we must have $$(TL)^3=\left(\frac{r_0L}{R}\right)^3=S_0\left(\frac{R}{\ell_p}\right)^{-8}>1.$$ Thus the AdS radius in Planck units is bounded by a polynomial in $S_0$ and we can neglect it in most equations.

This means that we must use quanta of exponentially low energy to send any messages; the absorption probability [\[Pabs\]](#Pabs){reference-type="eqref" reference="Pabs"} will thus be exponentially small.
It is still possible to send a message, but we must try many times.

For one thing even if the "true" $\alpha$ could be decreased by algorithms, our discussion below equation [\[entguess\]](#entguess){reference-type="eqref" reference="entguess"} suggests that, because of coarse-graining, $\alpha$ should be *increased* by some order one factor.
[^4]: The reader should not be confused by us writing $e^{2S_0}$ here and $2^{2n}$ there.

From the AMPS argument however we know that to have a smooth horizon it must be that there are some operators just outside the horizon, which act on what we've been calling $B$, measurements of which need to be close to perfectly correlated measurements of some of the behind-the-horizon $A_n$'s.
